analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2003 capital gains tax cuts permanent and cuts the corporate capital gains rate to 15%.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in April 2005, never received a vote, and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2003 tax law lowered the tax rate on investment profits (capital gains) for individuals, but only temporarily. This bill would have made those lower rates permanent, collapsed the individual rate structure into a flat 15%, and cut the corporate capital gains rate from 35% to 15%. Because investment gains flow mostly to households that own stocks and other assets, the tax savings would have gone mainly to wealthier taxpayers, while the federal government would have collected less revenue. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with taxable investment gains — overwhelmingly those in higher income brackets, since most capital gains are realized by stock and asset owners at the top of the income scale — and corporations, whose rate on capital gains would drop from 35% to 15%.

how_it_helps.text: Makes permanent the reduced individual capital gains rates enacted in 2003, which were scheduled to expire, by repealing the sunset provision of the 2003 tax law [S2][S3].
Replaces the tiered individual capital gains rate structure with a single flat 15% rate on net capital gain, simplifying the tax code for investors [S2][S3].
Cuts the maximum corporate capital gains tax rate from 35% to 15% and applies the same reduced rate to related withholding provisions [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Permanently lowering rates on investment profits reduces federal revenue, which must be made up through other taxes, more borrowing, or less spending — costs borne broadly by taxpayers and by anyone depending on federally funded programs.

drawbacks.text: Because capital gains income is concentrated among higher-income households, a permanent lower rate directs its largest dollar benefits to the wealthiest taxpayers while shrinking the revenue available for other priorities [S2][S3].
Making the cut permanent removes the built-in expiration date that Congress could later revisit, locking in the lower rates regardless of future budget conditions [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill simplifies the tax code and gives investors a permanent, lower rate on gains, but the benefits are concentrated among households and corporations that realize capital gains — a group skewed heavily toward the top of the income distribution — and the cost is a permanent loss of federal revenue. For most working households, the direct benefit is small or zero.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative David Dreier of California, joined by Representative Phil English of Pennsylvania, introduced the bill on April 6, 2005 [S1][S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
The committee took no further action; fifteen Republican representatives cosponsored the bill, but it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote [S4][S5].
The bill expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, no permanent capital gains rate cut was enacted; federal revenue was not reduced, and taxpayers broadly avoided the cost, while investors and corporations did not receive the additional rate cut they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal taxpayers generally; investors gained nothing

for.name: Rep. David Dreier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor [S1][S3][S5].

for.name: Rep. Phil English
for.role: Original co-lead, member of Ways and Means
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced [S3].

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax bills
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action; the bill never reached a committee markup or floor vote [S5].

against.name: Rep. Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman, never scheduled the bill for a markup or advanced it out of committee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. All 16 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, but the committee's inaction cannot be attributed to a party split since no vote occurred [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have permanently locked in a 15% top rate on investment gains, with the largest dollar savings going to households that realize the most capital gains — concentrated at the top of the income scale. The cost shows up as lower federal revenue shared by everyone else.
The corporate capital gains rate would have dropped from 35% to 15%, roughly a 57% cut in the rate on corporate investment profits, though corporations rarely realize large capital gains.
